prompt: Which of the four does no work of its own?
hint: Three of them calculate or remember. One of them is where that happens.

choices.text: The memory
choices.why: It holds what is being worked on, which is work of a kind.

choices.text: The storage
choices.why: It keeps what survives the power going, which is also a job.

choices.text: The processor
choices.why: It is the part that carries out every instruction.

choices.text: The motherboard
choices.why: It calculates nothing and remembers nothing; it is where the other three are.

prompt: A document has been typed and not saved. Where does it exist?
hint: One of the four is erased when the power goes.

choices.text: In memory, and nowhere else
choices.why: Which is why a power cut takes it.

choices.text: In the processor's registers
choices.why: Those hold a handful of values, not a document.

choices.text: In storage, waiting to be named
choices.why: Nothing reaches storage until it is saved.

choices.text: In both memory and storage
choices.why: Saving is what puts it in the second one.

prompt: Which part keeps its contents when the machine is switched off?

choices.text: The processor
choices.why: It holds only what it is working on at that instant.

choices.text: The memory
choices.why: Memory is volatile: the power going empties it.

choices.text: The motherboard
choices.why: It connects the others and holds no data of its own.

choices.text: The storage
choices.why: That is the property that distinguishes it.

prompt: Match each part to what it is for.
Which of these are true of memory?

choices.text: The processor reads it far faster than storage
choices.why: About a thousand times faster.

choices.text: It is larger than storage on a typical machine
choices.why: It is very much smaller.

choices.text: It is where the saved files live
choices.why: Saved files are in storage.

choices.text: It is emptied whenever the power goes
choices.why: That is what volatile means.

prompt: What does a core count tell you that a clock speed does not?
hint: One number is about speed and the other is about how many at once.

choices.text: How many steps each second the processor takes
choices.why: That is exactly what the clock speed says.

choices.text: How many instructions run at the same instant
choices.why: Each core is a processor in its own right.

choices.text: How much power it draws when loaded
choices.why: Related in practice, but not what the count means.

choices.text: How much cache the processor carries
choices.why: Cache is a separate figure and often unquoted.

prompt: A program that cannot be split runs on a 4-core 3 GHz machine and on a 1-core 5 GHz machine. Which finishes first?
hint: Work that does not split uses one core whatever the box says.

choices.text: The four-core machine
choices.why: Three of its cores sit idle; the fourth is slower.

choices.text: They finish at the same moment
choices.why: The clocks differ, so the single core in use differs.

choices.text: The one-core machine
choices.why: Only one core does the work, and its clock is higher.

choices.text: It depends on the memory fitted
choices.why: Memory is not what this question changes.

prompt: In `Core i5-13400`, which piece says how recent the design is?

choices.text: i5
choices.why: That is the tier — roughly, how much of it there is.
The generation, and only comparable within one brand.
The position inside the generation.

choices.text: Core
choices.why: The product family name.

prompt: Why has clock speed barely moved in twenty years?

choices.text: The manufacturers agreed a shared ceiling
choices.why: No such agreement exists.

choices.text: Memory stopped being able to keep up
choices.why: Memory is a real bottleneck, but not the reason clocks stalled.

choices.text: Programs stopped being written to need it
choices.why: Plenty of work is still bound by single-core speed.

choices.text: Past a point it makes heat faster than speed
choices.why: Which is why the growth moved to core counts.

prompt: A current i5 against an i7 from six years ago, at general work:
hint: Age moves a processor further than tier does.

choices.text: The current i5 tends to win
choices.why: Six generations is a wider gap than one tier.

choices.text: They land close enough to call even
choices.why: The generations are too far apart for that.

choices.text: The clock speeds decide it
choices.why: Clock speed is the least informative of the three.

choices.text: The older i7 tends to win
choices.why: Its tier was higher in a much older generation.

prompt: What is swapping?

choices.text: Exchanging a memory module for a larger one
choices.why: That is an upgrade, not what the word means here.

choices.text: Moving a running program between cores
choices.why: That is scheduling, and it is cheap.

choices.text: Clearing the memory a closed program held
choices.why: That happens, and it is not swapping.

choices.text: Writing part of memory out to storage
choices.why: And reading it back when that window is clicked.

prompt: A machine is slow, the disk light is constant, and the processor graph is near idle. What is happening?
hint: Look at which part is busy, not at which is fast.

choices.text: The processor is too slow for the work
choices.why: Then the processor graph would be pinned, not idle.

choices.text: The storage drive is failing
choices.why: Possible, but the idle processor points at swapping first.

choices.text: A program is stuck in a tight loop
choices.why: A loop would keep one core at full.

choices.text: It ran out of memory and is swapping
choices.why: Busy storage plus an idle processor is the signature.

prompt: Which symptom points at swapping rather than at a slow processor?

choices.text: One program takes ages to finish
choices.why: That is the shape of a processor-bound task.

choices.text: Starting the machine is slow
choices.why: Startup is mostly storage, swapping or not.

choices.text: Switching between windows hurts
choices.why: Each switch drags something back off storage.

choices.text: The fan is running loudly
choices.why: Heat follows work, and both cases make it.

prompt: A machine at its memory ceiling. Which purchase helps most?

choices.text: More memory in it
choices.why: You are buying the absence of the swapping, not speed.

choices.text: A larger monitor
choices.why: It changes nothing about the ceiling.

choices.text: A faster processor
choices.why: It would spend the same time waiting.

choices.text: A second drive
choices.why: More room to swap into is not less swapping.

prompt: Roughly how many nanoseconds does a processor wait to read something from memory?
hint: The lesson gives it as one of five round figures.

prompt: Memory is ___, which means its contents are gone when the power is.
What makes a hard disk slow to reach a particular file?

choices.text: Its chips are of an older generation
choices.why: A hard disk stores on platters, not chips.

choices.text: Its connection to the motherboard is narrow
choices.why: Connections matter, but the arm is the larger cost.

choices.text: It searches every file in turn
choices.why: It does not; it is told where to go.

choices.text: An arm and a platter have to move
choices.why: That wait is seek time, and it is mechanical.

prompt: An eight-year-old laptop gets an SSD and feels new. What got faster?
hint: Nothing in the list of four changed its speed.

choices.text: The processor, once it stopped throttling
choices.why: Heat is unrelated to the change made.

choices.text: Nothing did — it simply waits less
choices.why: The processor was always idle, waiting on the disk.

choices.text: The memory, which the SSD adds to
choices.why: An SSD does not add memory.

choices.text: The connection to the motherboard
choices.why: The connection is the same one the disk used.

prompt: Which pair of words describes the same kind of thing?

choices.text: SSD and NVMe
choices.why: One is what it is made of, the other how it connects.

choices.text: HDD and SATA
choices.why: Same mismatch, the other way round.

choices.text: SSD and capacity
choices.why: One is a technology, the other a size.

choices.text: SATA and NVMe
choices.why: Both are how a drive is connected.

prompt: Which are true of an SSD compared with a hard disk?

choices.text: It keeps data when the power goes
choices.why: True, but hard disks do that too.

choices.text: It costs less for each gigabyte
choices.why: It costs several times more.

choices.text: It reaches a file a hundred times sooner
choices.why: 0.1 ms against 10 ms.

choices.text: It has no moving parts at all
choices.why: It is memory chips.

prompt: `1 TB HDD` against `512 GB SSD` at the same price. Which reads a file sooner?

choices.text: The HDD, with more room to work in
choices.why: Capacity is not speed.

choices.text: The SSD, and by a long way
choices.why: By roughly a hundred times, and the capacity is the persuasion.

choices.text: Neither — they are the same thing
choices.why: They are two different technologies.

choices.text: It depends on how big the file is
choices.why: The gap is in reaching it at all.

prompt: Put these in order, nearest to the processor first.
On the scale where one nanosecond is one second, how long is a read from memory?

choices.text: About two minutes
choices.why: A hundred nanoseconds, scaled.

choices.text: About four months
choices.why: That is a hard disk.

choices.text: About a day and a half
choices.why: That is an SSD.

choices.text: About five seconds
choices.why: That is cache.

prompt: Which level is inside the processor and cannot be bought separately?

choices.text: Memory
choices.why: Memory is modules you can add.

choices.text: The SSD
choices.why: A drive is a separate component.

choices.text: Cache
choices.why: It comes with the processor and is often unquoted.

choices.text: The page file
choices.why: That is space on storage, not a level of its own.

prompt: Two processors, same clock and same core count, differ by a third in real work. What most likely differs?

choices.text: How many watts each draws
choices.why: Power follows the work rather than producing it.

choices.text: The memory beside them
choices.why: The question holds the rest of the machine fixed.

choices.text: How much cache each one has
choices.why: More cache means reaching memory less often.

choices.text: The brand printed on them
choices.why: A brand is not a mechanism.

prompt: "Close some tabs" and "put an SSD in it" are the same advice about what?
hint: Both are about a boundary rather than about speed.

choices.text: Reducing how much electricity the machine uses
choices.why: Neither is about power.

choices.text: Making the processor hold a higher clock
choices.why: Neither changes the clock.

choices.text: Not falling a level, or falling less far
choices.why: Which is the whole of making a machine feel fast.

choices.text: Freeing space on the drive for more files
choices.why: Closing tabs frees memory, not drive space.

prompt: Scaled so that one nanosecond is one second, a read from a hard disk is about how many months?
Match each level to its scaled human time.
In `16 GB DDR4-3200`, which part of the machine is being described?

choices.text: The processor
choices.why: That is quoted as a model name.

choices.text: Storage
choices.why: Storage is quoted as SSD or HDD.

choices.text: The graphics
choices.why: Graphics is quoted separately.

choices.text: Memory
choices.why: DDR4 is a memory generation.

prompt: Of the three questions the lesson gives, which is asked first?

choices.text: Is the processor a recent one?
choices.why: Third, and the tier matters less than the age.

choices.text: Is the graphics built in?
choices.why: A later lesson's question.

choices.text: Is there at least 16 GB of memory?
choices.why: Second, and only once storage is settled.

choices.text: Is the storage solid state?
choices.why: Nothing else in the list rescues a machine that fails it.

prompt: `32 GB RAM · 1 TB HDD` on a budget machine. What is wrong with the arrangement?
hint: One number is generous and one is the four-month level.

choices.text: A terabyte is too little room for the price
choices.why: It is plenty of room.

choices.text: The money went to memory, not to the slow part
choices.why: 16 GB and an SSD would feel like another category.

choices.text: The two parts do not work together
choices.why: They work together; the balance is the problem.

choices.text: Thirty-two gigabytes is never useful to anybody
choices.why: It is useful — just not before an SSD.

prompt: What does `Up to 4.6 GHz` describe?

choices.text: A short burst, on a single core
choices.why: The sustained figure is lower.

choices.text: The clock it holds under sustained load
choices.why: That is the base clock, and it is lower.

choices.text: The total across every core at once
choices.why: Clock speed is per core, not a total.

choices.text: The fastest memory the board accepts
choices.why: Memory speed is quoted with the memory.

prompt: Why does the specification matter more when buying a phone than a desktop?

choices.text: A phone has a different set of parts in it
choices.why: The same four roles are in both.

choices.text: A phone's specification is less honestly written
choices.why: The difference is what you can fix later.

choices.text: Its memory and storage cannot be changed later
choices.why: On a desktop both are a screwdriver away.

choices.text: A phone costs more than a desktop does
choices.why: Price is not what the question turns on.

prompt: The three questions in order: is the storage an ___, is there at least ___ GB of memory, and is the processor recent?
Why does a full memory make a machine feel slow rather than simply refuse to open anything?

choices.text: It compresses everything where it already is
choices.why: Some systems do compress, and the fall is still the point.

choices.text: It drops the processor to a lower clock to cope
choices.why: Clock speed is not adjusted for this.

choices.text: It closes the programs you are not looking at
choices.why: They stay open; parts of them move.

choices.text: It borrows storage to stand in for the room
choices.why: And storage is a level further down.

prompt: How much memory does the lesson call the sensible default for a general machine?

choices.text: 8 GB
choices.why: Workable, and you will meet the ceiling.

choices.text: 4 GB
choices.why: Below the lesson's range entirely.

choices.text: 32 GB
choices.why: For video editing, virtual machines and large datasets.

choices.text: 16 GB
choices.why: Browser, office suite and a video call at once.

prompt: About how many milliseconds does a hard disk take to reach a particular track?
Why is calling the motherboard a component misleading?

choices.text: It is the building, not a worker
choices.why: It calculates nothing and remembers nothing.

choices.text: It is far too small a thing to matter
choices.why: It is the largest object in the case.

choices.text: It is really a part of the processor
choices.why: The processor plugs into it.

choices.text: It is optional on a modern machine
choices.why: Nothing works without it.

prompt: Put the pieces of `Core i5-13400` in the order they appear.
Why leave some of an SSD empty?

choices.text: A backup needs somewhere to be written
choices.why: True of a plan, and not the mechanism here.

choices.text: Below a tenth free it runs out of blocks
choices.why: The one place capacity and speed touch.

choices.text: The system refuses further writes to it
choices.why: It writes; it just writes more slowly.

choices.text: A drive close to full will run hotter
choices.why: Heat is not what changes.

prompt: Which of these live inside the processor?

choices.text: Registers
choices.why: The handful of values in use this instant.

choices.text: Cache
choices.why: A small fast copy of recently used memory.

choices.text: The page file
choices.why: Space on storage.

choices.text: Memory
choices.why: Modules on the board, outside the processor.

prompt: Saving a document is which movement?

choices.text: From memory to storage
choices.why: Which is why it then survives the power going.

choices.text: From the processor to memory
choices.why: That happens constantly and is not saving.

choices.text: From storage to memory
choices.why: That is opening it.

choices.text: From memory to the motherboard
choices.why: The motherboard holds nothing.

prompt: How many billion steps a second does a processor quoted at 3.2 GHz take?
A listing gives capacity in large type and never says SSD or HDD. What should you assume?

choices.text: That the capacity makes the question irrelevant
choices.why: Capacity says nothing about the wait.

choices.text: That the seller simply forgot to write it
choices.why: Perhaps — and the question still stands.

choices.text: That it must be an SSD, being the standard
choices.why: Cheap machines still ship hard disks.

choices.text: That it is the first thing to find out
choices.why: The first of the three questions is unanswered.

prompt: What is the single sentence the lesson offers for making a computer feel fast?

choices.text: Buy the highest clock speed you can
choices.why: Clock speed is the least informative figure.

choices.text: Keep the drive as empty as possible
choices.why: A real effect, and a small one.

choices.text: Keep work from falling down a level
choices.why: Which is what every piece of advice in it reduces to.

choices.text: Prefer more cores over faster ones
choices.why: It depends entirely on whether the work splits.
